summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator — Window Finder is a web-based prototype designed to identify promising lunar landing locations and times based on sunlight, communication with Earth, and available power.

Using NASA/JPL astronomical data, NASA lunar terrain datasets, and USGS reference grids, the tool is designed to compare nearby sites against user-defined mission requirements. Hourly simulations evaluate sunlight, Earth visibility, and battery charge, while interactive maps, rankings, and countdowns help users understand potential landing windows.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting lunar conditions to practical mission decisions: where to land, when to arrive, and how long a spacecraft can operate within its limits. Its distinctive approach considers terrain, energy, and communication together, since a sunlit location may still lose contact with Earth or experience battery shortages.

Window Finder aims to make early mission planning more accessible while helping students and the public understand the constraints that shape lunar exploration.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator — Window Finder is a web-based prototype designed to help mission planners, students, and the public explore a practical lunar exploration question: Where and when should a spacecraft land to maintain sunlight, power, and communication with Earth?

Users select a proposed landing location, a date range, and mission requirements such as mission duration, maximum darkness, maximum communication outage, solar-panel output, battery capacity, and power consumption. The system is designed to compare nearby landing locations and times by simulating sunlight, Earth visibility, and battery charge hour by hour. Its interface brings these results together through maps, rankings, horizon views, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset.

The project combines NASA/JPL Horizons astronomical data, NASA lunar terrain datasets, and the USGS Lunar Grid Reference System. Terrain matters because nearby ridges can block the Sun or Earth even when they are above the Moon’s theoretical horizon. By considering local terrain alongside mission requirements, Window Finder aims to reveal differences that a conventional map cannot show.

Its creative feature is the shift from simply displaying lunar conditions to finding usable mission windows. A location with abundant sunlight may still experience communication outages or exhaust a spacecraft’s battery. Window Finder evaluates these conditions together and uses an explicit ranking order: prioritize options that meet mission limits, then compare battery reserves, simultaneous sunlight and Earth visibility, distance, and communication continuity. A landing-time slider lets users explore how a schedule change affects their options.

We developed the project using Python for data preparation and JavaScript with React and Vite for the web application. The geospatial pipeline uses NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, and GeoPandas. The interface stack includes Tailwind CSS, ECharts, and globe.gl. Heavy terrain calculations are prepared in advance, while browser-based calculations use Web Workers to keep the interface responsive. The architecture targets static hosting on Vercel and requires no specialized hardware. Claude Code assisted with scaffolding, implementation, and documentation, with contributions recorded in the repository.

Our design considerations included scientific accuracy, transparent assumptions, accessibility, performance, and reproducibility. We distinguish mock data from real observations, document sources and resolution limits, and identify when terrain information is unavailable. The implemented astronomical geometry has been checked against JPL Horizons, while broader terrain validation and integration remain in progress.

The intended impact is to make lunar mission constraints easier to understand and compare, supporting early exploration of landing alternatives while giving learners an interactive way to see how terrain, orbital geometry, and energy needs shape a mission.
